items.title: Build Live Apps in Cursor
items.excerpt: Agents have lowered the cost of writing code, but most apps and tools that users build never make it off of localhost. Now, you can build live apps directly in Cursor and share them with a link. Describe what you want to create and Cursor will handle the rest: build the app, set up a database, configure auth, and deploy it. With this release, anyone in your org can now build useful tools for their work and share them with teammates. Update Cursor to try it out. How it works To get started, kick off a cloud agent and tell it explicitly that you want to build an app. Cursor will scaffold the web app, spin up a Postgres database if needed, set up authentication behind Cursor SSO, and provision hosting. If the app needs to connect to your systems, like a data warehouse, Cursor will ask for the secrets it needs. When you go to publish your app, you pick a unique domain and Cursor gets you back a live link. At Cursor, users across sales, operations, legal, finance, and engineering are building internal apps. Some of the most useful ones are: Internal ops tools for event registration, account assignments, and desk seating Multimedia presentations for customers that combine slides, videos, and interactive demos Training, enablement, and onboarding experiences for new hires Live dashboards and tools for sales teams to understand their pipeline and opportunities Portals to manage engineering services Cursor can deploy apps from new or existing repos across Cursor Origin and GitHub. Support for other git providers like GitLab is coming soon. Controls and guardrails When you publish an app, Cursor will run deterministic and agentic security checks to catch common issues, like secrets written in app files or exposed credentials. If a check fails, the agent tells you what it needs to fix. Nothing goes live until the checks pass and y
items.why_it_matters: Cursor can now build, deploy and share full apps with a database and auth from a prompt. This competes with MVP-style work and changes what clients expect, so it is worth watching for build-vs-buy advice.

items.title: New pull request overview page in public preview
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: On a long pull request, checking what’s blocking often means scrolling past dozens of comments and timeline events just to reach the merge box. And once you’re there, you still need to work out what to do next. As people need to review more and more pull requests, time spent scrolling adds up. So we’ve begun to rethink the entire experience, beginning with addressing a familiar challenge: finding what’s blocking progress and determining what to do next. Today, we’re introducing the Overview page as an opt-in public preview, with rollout continuing through the weekend. It brings merge status and next available actions to the top of the page in a compact readiness summary. It’s the first step toward making pull requests easier to follow as code, conversations, and reviews evolve. The merge box, distilled We’re starting with the merge box, the place developers go to see whether a pull request can move forward. Rather than just moving it higher, we’ve also redesigned it to show the same information in less than half the space. Explore the supporting signals: A compact view of checks, comments, and approvals keeps the context nearby without making every detail compete for attention. Address what’s blocking: Take action to move the pull request forward, such as updating your branch. See if it’s ready to merge: Check merge readiness and merge when requirements are met. Start with the summary, then follow the detail that matters to your next step (e.g., get to failing checks, see who still needs to approve, or open the relevant comments). Keep your place. Focus your attention. This first preview also introduces more ways to catch up on activity and focus the conversation so you can spend less time finding your place. Narrow the conversation: Filter for unresolved conversations or comments you wrote to find open questions or follow up on your feedback. Read the latest comments first: Sort comments from newest to oldest instead of starting with the earliest discussion. Catch
items.why_it_matters: New GitHub PR overview page puts merge status and blockers in one place, which could speed up our heavy review workflow for agent-generated PRs. Opt-in preview.

items.title: Secret scanning upgrades detectors, adds SpaceX as partner
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: This update expands secret scanning’s detection coverage: New partner: SpaceX is now a secret scanning partner. New detector: GitHub now detects starlink_public_api_v2_secret. Upgraded detectors: Alibaba, AWS, Google, OpenVSX, Pydantic Services, and Tencent detectors include additional false-positive filtering. New secret scanning partners The following provider joined the secret scanning partnership program. When one of their secrets is found in a public repository, GitHub forwards it to the partner so they can revoke or rotate the credential before it can be abused. Provider Secret type SpaceX starlink_public_api_v2_secret Detectors added Secret scanning now automatically detects the following new secret type in your repositories. Provider Secret type SpaceX starlink_public_api_v2_secret Partner secrets are automatically reported to the secret issuer when found in public repositories through the secret scanning partnership program. User secrets generate secret scanning alerts when found in public or private repositories. False positives reduced The following detector improvements reduce false-positive matches for supported secrets. Provider Secret type Improvement Alibaba alibaba_cloud_access_key_id Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion secrets. AWS aws_access_key_id Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion secrets. AWS aws_session_token Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion secrets. AWS aws_temporary_access_key_id Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion secrets. Google google_cloud_storage_access_key_secret Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion key identifiers. Google google_cloud_storage_service_account_access_key_id Suppress unpaired matches when dictionary filtering removes all qualifying companion secrets. Google google_cloud_storage
items.why_it_matters: Incremental GitHub secret scanning update with fewer false positives for AWS and Google detectors; useful background for repo hygiene but no action required.
